title: Setting Up Your First Proxy in 5 Minutes
body: Getting started with proxies doesn't have to be complicated. In this guide, we'll walk you through the entire process—from signing up to making your first request through a proxy—in under five minutes. Whether you're a marketer gathering competitive data, a developer testing your application, or a sneaker enthusiast trying to cop the latest release, this tutorial will have you up and running fast. ## Getting Your Proxy Credentials Before you can start using a proxy, you need your authentication credentials. After signing up for a Styxproxy account, getting your proxy credentials is straightforward: 1. **Log in to your dashboard** at styxproxy.com 2. Navigate to the **"Proxies"** section in the left sidebar 3. Click on **"Generate Credentials"** if you haven't already 4. Copy your **Username** and **Password**—these are the keys to your proxy network Your credentials will look something like this: ``` Username: your_username Password: your_secure_password ``` You'll use these credentials with every proxy request you make. Keep them secure—never share them publicly or commit them to version control. ## Making Your First Proxy Request Now for the exciting part: using your proxy. We'll show you two common methods—curl for quick testing and Python with the requests library for programmatic use. ### Using curl The quickest way to test your proxy is with curl from the command line. Replace the placeholders with your actual credentials: ```bash curl -x "http://your_username:your_password@proxy.styxproxy.com:8000" \ -I https://httpbin.org/ip ``` Let's break down what's happening: - `-x` tells curl to use a proxy - `http://username:password@host:port` is the proxy URL format - `-I` sends a HEAD request (just headers, no body) - `https://httpbin.org/ip` returns your IP address so you can verify the proxy is working If successful, you'll see the response headers including your proxy-assigned IP address. The `httpbin.org/ip` endpoint is incredibly useful for testing—it simply returns the IP address that made the request, confirming your proxy is working correctly. ### Using Python with Requests For more complex projects, you'll want to use Python. The requests library makes proxy integration seamless: ```python import requests # Your proxy credentials proxy_url = "http://username:password@proxy.styxproxy.com:8000" # Define proxies dictionary proxies = { "http": proxy_url, "https": proxy_url, } # Make a request through the proxy try: response = requests.get( "https://httpbin.org/ip", proxies=proxies, timeout=10 ) print(f"Status Code: {response.status_code}") print(f"Response: {response.json()}") except requests.exceptions.RequestException as e: print(f"Request failed: {e}") ``` A few important notes about this code: 1. **Both protocols**: We define both `http` and `https` proxies to ensure requests work regardless of the URL scheme 2. **Error handling**: Always wrap proxy requests in try-except blocks—network issues are more common with proxies 3. **Timeout**: Set reasonable timeouts (10 seconds is usually sufficient) to prevent your code from hanging If you're making multiple requests, you can create a session object that reuses the connection: ```python import requests session = requests.Session() session.proxies = { "http": "http://username:password@proxy.styxproxy.com:8000", "https": "http://username:password@proxy.styxproxy.com:8000", } # All requests through this session use the proxy for i in range(5): response = session.get("https://httpbin.org/ip") print(f"Request {i+1}: {response.json()}") ``` ### Rotating Through Multiple Proxies If you have multiple proxies and want to rotate between them, here's how: ```python import requests import random # List of proxy credentials proxies_list = [ "http://user1:pass1@proxy.styxproxy.com:8000", "http://user2:pass2@proxy.styxproxy.com:8000", "http://user3:pass3@proxy.styxproxy.com:8000", ] def get_random_proxy(): """Return a random proxy from the list.""" return random.choice(proxies_list) def make_proxy_request(url): """Make a request using a randomly selected proxy.""" proxy = get_random_proxy() proxies = { "http": proxy, "https": proxy, } response = requests.get(url, proxies=proxies, timeout=10) return response # Make 10 requests, each using a different proxy for i in range(10): response = make_proxy_request("https://httpbin.org/ip") print(f"Request {i+1}: {response.json()}") ``` This approach is useful for tasks that require making many requests without getting rate-limited—rotating proxies spreads the load across multiple IP addresses. ## Configuring Proxies in Your Browser Sometimes you need to route your browser traffic through a proxy rather than a specific application. Here's how to do it in the most popular browsers: ### Chrome Chrome uses your system's proxy settings on Windows and macOS: 1. Click the three dots menu → **Settings** 2. Scroll down and click **Advanced** 3. Under the "System" section, click **Open your computer's proxy settings** 4. Toggle on "Use a proxy server" and enter your Styxproxy details: - Address: `proxy.styxproxy.com` - Port: `8000` 5. Save and restart Chrome For Windows 10/11: Go to Settings → Network & Internet → Proxy → Manual proxy setup For macOS: Go to System Preferences → Network → Advanced → Proxies → Manual Proxy Configuration ### Firefox Firefox has its own proxy settings independent of the system: 1. Click the menu (three lines) → **Settings** 2. Search for "proxy" in the settings search 3. Click **Settings** under Network Settings 4. Select **Manual proxy configuration** 5. Enter your proxy details: - HTTP Proxy: `proxy.styxproxy.com` - Port: `8000` 6. Check "Also use this proxy for HTTPS" 7. Click **OK** to save Firefox is particularly useful for proxy testing because you can easily toggle it on and off without affecting other applications. ### Testing Your Browser Proxy To verify your browser proxy is working: 1. Visit [httpbin.org/ip](https://httpbin.org/ip) 2. The IP address displayed should be different from your actual IP 3. If you see your real IP, double-check your proxy settings ## Verifying Your Proxy Connection Before diving into your actual work, verify everything is configured correctly: 1. **Test with curl/Python**: Make a test request to httpbin.org/ip as shown above 2. **Check IP visibility**: Visit an "what is my IP" website through your browser 3. **Test both protocols**: Ensure both HTTP and HTTPS work through the proxy 4. **Check location**: Use a geolocation service to confirm your proxy IP is in the expected region If you encounter issues, common culprits include: - **Authentication errors**: Double-check your username and password - **Wrong port**: Verify you're using port 8000 (or the port specified in your dashboard) - **Protocol mismatch**: Some proxies only support certain protocols—ensure your URL scheme matches ## Start Your Journey with Styxproxy Congratulations! You've successfully set up your first proxy and made requests through it. You're now ready to use proxies for web scraping, competitive research, automation, or any other project you have in mind. title: Nigeria Proxy Market: Why Local IPs Matter for Some Use Cases
body: Nigeria represents one of the most dynamic and underserved proxy markets in Africa. With over 200 million people, a rapidly growing digital economy, and increasing internet penetration, the demand for Nigerian IP addresses has surged across multiple industries. Whether you're a marketer looking to localize campaigns, a developer testing geo-restricted applications, or a business expanding into West African markets, understanding the nuances of Nigeria's proxy landscape can give you a significant competitive edge. ## Understanding Nigeria's Proxy Market The Nigerian proxy market has matured considerably over the past five years. What started primarily as a tool for circumvention has evolved into a sophisticated infrastructure supporting legitimate business operations. The market is characterized by a mix of international providers offering Nigerian exit nodes and local providers operating residential and data center IPs within the country. Several factors make Nigeria particularly interesting for proxy services. The country's telecommunications infrastructure, while still developing, has expanded significantly with multiple mobile network operators competing for market share. This competition has driven down data costs and increased accessibility, creating a larger pool of residential IPs. However, the supply of quality Nigerian proxies remains limited compared to more established markets like the US or UK, which means prices tend to run higher and availability can be inconsistent. From a pricing perspective, Nigerian proxies typically command a premium. Residential proxies in Nigeria often cost 20-40% more than equivalent IPs from more saturated markets. This premium reflects the operational challenges of maintaining quality IP infrastructure in the region, including power instability, network reliability issues, and the complexity of working with local internet service providers. ## Why Nigerian Proxies Are in High Demand The demand for Nigerian IP addresses stems from several converging factors. First, Nigeria has become Africa's largest e-commerce market, with companies increasingly needing to verify how their platforms appear to local users. Second, the country's financial technology sector has exploded, with mobile banking and payment platforms requiring robust geo-verification. Third, digital advertising networks need Nigerian impressions to serve relevant ads and prevent fraud. Payment localization has also driven significant demand. Nigeria's Central Bank requires international businesses to process certain transactions in local currency (Naira, NGN), and many payment processors gate their full functionality behind Nigerian IP addresses. Companies looking to integrate with platforms like Paystack, Flutterwave, or local bank APIs often need Nigerian IPs to access test environments or verify that their integrations work correctly for end users. For businesses accepting payments in Naira, having a local IP address helps avoid the friction that comes with international transaction flags. Payment providers often review transactions more heavily when they originate from foreign IPs, leading to higher decline rates. Using Nigerian proxies for payment processing workflows can reduce false positives and improve approval rates for legitimate transactions. The tax compliance landscape has also become more complex. The Federal Inland Revenue Service (FIRS) has implemented digital reporting requirements, and businesses operating in Nigeria increasingly need to demonstrate local presence for tax purposes. While proxies aren't a substitute for proper legal registration, they do help teams access Nigerian tax portals and compliance platforms that restrict foreign access. ## Use Cases for Nigeria-Based Proxies The practical applications for Nigerian proxies span multiple sectors. Digital marketers use them to verify ad delivery, check localized search results, and monitor how campaigns perform in the Nigerian market. Without a local IP, it's difficult to accurately see what users in Lagos or Abuja actually see when they search or browse. E-commerce businesses use Nigerian proxies to test their checkout flows, verify pricing display, and ensure that shipping calculations work correctly for different Nigerian states. Many international retailers launching in Nigeria use proxies to debug their platforms before going live, catching issues that would otherwise only surface when real customers encounter them. For developers and QA teams, Nigerian proxies are essential when building applications that integrate with local services. Testing Nigeria-specific APIs, verifying SMS delivery flows, and debugging location-based features all require local IP addresses. The complexity of Nigeria's banking system, with its multiple settlement windows and varying gateway behaviors, makes local testing particularly important. Sneaker releases and ticket purchasing represent another common use case. Local drop releases in Nigeria often implement queueing systems or geographic restrictions. Having Nigerian IPs helps buyers participate in these releases without being automatically blocked by IP-based filtering. Market researchers use Nigerian proxies to gather data from local sources, monitor competitor pricing, and track digital trends in the region. The ability to appear as a local user provides access to content and insights that would otherwise be unavailable or would require expensive on-the-ground resources. ## Challenges in the Nigerian Proxy Space Operating proxy infrastructure in Nigeria comes with real challenges that affect both providers and users. Power infrastructure remains unreliable in many areas, which means residential IPs can go offline unexpectedly. Network congestion during peak hours can degrade performance significantly. And the relative scarcity of high-quality Nigerian IPs means that when you find a reliable provider, the relationship is worth maintaining. Provider reliability varies dramatically. Some providers offer impressive speed tests but suffer from poor IP rotation practices, leading to blocks. Others maintain consistent IPs but struggle with uptime. The key is finding a provider that understands the local infrastructure and has established relationships with Nigerian network operators. Payment and billing add another layer of complexity. Many international proxy providers don't accept Naira payments, requiring users to pay in USD or other hard currencies. This creates foreign exchange risk and can complicate budgeting for Nigerian businesses. Some local providers have emerged to fill this gap, offering Naira-based billing, but they often have smaller IP pools or less sophisticated infrastructure. Regulatory uncertainty also affects the market. Nigeria's government has at various times discussed restrictions on VPN and proxy services, though enforcement has been inconsistent. Users should stay informed about current regulations and work with providers who maintain compliance frameworks. ## Finding Reliable Nigerian Proxy Providers When evaluating Nigerian proxy providers, several factors matter more than they might in other markets. First, ask about their network partnerships. Providers with direct relationships with MTN, Airtel, Glo, or 9mobile can offer more stable residential IPs than those relying on third-party networks. Second, test performance during Nigerian peak hours (typically evenings local time). Residential proxy speeds that look fine during off-peak hours may become unusable when network congestion hits. The best providers publish performance metrics and offer trial periods specifically for Nigerian IPs. Third, verify billing options. If you need to pay in Naira, look for providers offering local payment methods including bank transfers, mobile money, or local payment gateways. Currency conversion fees add up, and the convenience of local billing often outweighs marginal savings on international pricing. Finally, check support responsiveness. Providers who understand the Nigerian market should be able to troubleshoot local connectivity issues and provide guidance on best practices for your specific use case. ## Styxproxy: Your Nigeria Proxy Solution At Styxproxy, we understand that Nigerian IPs serve critical business functions that go beyond simple geo-spoofing. title: How to Choose a Proxy Provider: 7 Questions to Ask
body: Finding a reliable proxy provider shouldn't feel like gambling. Whether you're managing multiple accounts, running automated tests, or scraping data at scale, the right provider can save you hours of frustration. The wrong one will cost you in blocked requests, slow speeds, and wasted budget. Here's what you need to ask before committing. ## 1. What IP Locations Do You Actually Need? Don't pay for coverage you won't use. Map out the geos your work requires — whether that's specific cities, countries, or regions — and verify the provider has IPs there. Some providers offer thousands of locations but have thin coverage in the regions that actually matter for your use case. Check whether they support residential, datacenter, or mobile IPs in those locations, since each type carries different trust levels with target websites. ## 2. How Are Your IPs Sourced and Rotated? This matters more than most people realize. Residential IPs come from real user devices and are harder to detect, but they can be slow and expensive. Datacenter IPs are faster and cheaper but get flagged more easily. Ask how often IPs rotate — some providers give you fresh IPs per request, others let you hold the same IP for hours. If you're managing accounts, sticky sessions matter. If you're scraping, aggressive rotation might be what you need. ## 3. What's Actually Included in Your Plan? Read the fine print before you sign up. Bandwidth limits, request quotas, and concurrent connection caps vary wildly between providers. Some charge extra for certain locations, API access, or geographic targeting features. Others bundle everything but throttle you once you hit a threshold. Get clear on what's unlimited versus what's metered, and factor in overage costs if you're running high-volume operations. ## 4. How Do You Handle Blocked Requests and Failed Connections? Every provider encounters blocks — it's inevitable. What separates good providers from bad ones is how they respond. Look for automatic IP replacement on failure, retry logic built into their API, or dedicated account managers who can whitelist your targets. Some providers offer dedicated support channels for enterprise users. Ask whether they monitor IP health and proactively replace bad IPs, or if you're left to figure it out on your own. ## 5. What Does Their Support Actually Look Like? A provider with fast, knowledgeable support can be the difference between a 10-minute fix and a 10-hour outage. Test their response time before committing — email their support with a technical question and see how long it takes to get a useful answer. Check whether they offer documentation, status pages, and community forums. If you're running critical operations, find out whether phone or Slack support is available. Cheap providers often skimp on support, and you'll feel it when something breaks at 2 AM. ## 6. Can You Integrate With Your Current Stack? If you're using Python, Node, Go, or a tool like Playwright, check whether the provider has official SDKs or clear API documentation. Some proxies work seamlessly with popular scraping frameworks; others require hacky workarounds. Verify authentication methods — API keys, username/password, or whitelisted IPs — and whether they support the protocols you need (HTTP, SOCKS5, etc.). Integration friction adds hidden time costs that pile up over time. ## 7. What's the Real Pricing Model? This is where many people get surprised. The advertised per-IP price often doesn't reflect total cost. Factor in bandwidth overages, location premiums, API call costs, and any add-ons you'll actually need. Some providers offer tiered pricing where the first few hundred IPs are cheap but scaling gets exponentially more expensive. Others charge flat rates regardless of volume. Calculate your projected usage across all variables and compare real costs, not headline prices. --- ## The Bottom Line Choosing a proxy provider comes down to matching their capabilities to your specific needs. Don't chase the cheapest option or the one with the most locations. Focus on the locations you need, the IP quality your use case demands, and whether the total cost aligns with your budget. If you want a provider that checks these boxes — competitive pricing, global coverage, reliable IPs, and responsive support — take a look at [Styxproxy](/products). We built our service to be straightforward: transparent pricing, clean IPs, and support that actually responds. No hidden fees, no guesswork.

title: Avoiding Proxy Bans: 5 Rules That Actually Work
body: Getting banned while using proxies is frustrating, expensive, and entirely preventable. Whether you're managing multiple accounts for marketing, running automated tests, or trying to cop limited-release sneakers, a single misstep can lock you out of platforms you've invested time and money into building. The good news? Most proxy bans aren't caused by sophisticated detection systems—they're caused by predictable, avoidable mistakes. This guide breaks down the five rules that actually work for staying undetected. These aren't theoretical suggestions; they're practical techniques you can implement immediately to dramatically reduce your ban risk. ## Why Do Accounts Get Banned When Using Proxies? Before diving into the rules, it helps to understand what triggers bans in the first place. Most platforms don't have AI systems hunting for proxy users specifically. Instead, they flag behavioral anomalies—patterns that don't match how normal humans (or even normal businesses) interact with their services. When you route traffic through a proxy, you're introducing variables that platforms can detect: IP addresses that don't match device fingerprints, geographic locations that shift impossibly fast, request patterns that exceed human capabilities, and authentication data that conflicts across sessions. The goal isn't to hide the fact that you're using a proxy—it's to make your activity look exactly like legitimate traffic from a real user. Understanding this distinction is crucial. You don't need to be invisible; you need to be invisible in the same way thousands of other users are invisible. Blend in, don't stand out. ## Rule 1: Always Warm Up Your IPs Before Heavy Use This is the single most ignored rule in proxy usage, and it costs people more bans than any other mistake. Imagine getting a brand-new phone, immediately trying to place 500 orders in an hour, and wondering why the retailer flags you—that's essentially what you're doing when you use a fresh IP for high-volume activity without warming it up first. IP warming means gradually increasing your activity level on a new IP address over several days or weeks, mimicking how a normal user would ramp up their activity. Start by using the IP for light browsing—checking email, reading content, casually browsing the target platform. After a few days, increase to minor actions: liking posts, viewing multiple pages, making occasional small queries. Only after a week or two should you attempt high-volume operations. Here's a practical example: if you're scaling sneaker purchases, don't start with ten checkout attempts on day one. Start with two or three visits to the site, add items to cart, maybe attempt one checkout, then gradually increase over a week. By the time you're attempting multiple purchases, the IP has established a legitimate-looking history. The same principle applies to residential proxies that haven't been used extensively. Even if the IP itself is clean, the lack of historical activity is a red flag to sophisticated detection systems. ## Rule 2: Implement Realistic Rate Limits and Request Delays Speed is the enemy of stealth. When you can execute tasks programmatically, there's a natural tendency to do them as fast as possible—but that's exactly what gets you caught. Human users can't click, load pages, and submit forms at machine speed, and platforms know this. Rate limiting isn't just about avoiding triggers on a single site. It's about respecting the natural pacing of human behavior. Between each significant action, implement randomized delays that mirror human timing. Instead of exactly 2 seconds between requests, vary between 1.5 and 4 seconds. Instead of submitting forms at the same millisecond every time, add random jitter. For example, when scraping product pages, don't request them in perfect sequence with identical timing. Add natural pauses—spend 30 seconds reading product details, scroll down, perhaps click to view an image before moving to the next page. These seemingly minor details create behavioral patterns that match real users. Most automated tools default to maximum speed for efficiency, but when you're trying to avoid bans, efficiency is the wrong priority. Slow down. The few extra seconds per action are trivial compared to the cost of losing your account. ## Rule 3: Match Your Proxy Location to Your Device and Session Data One of the fastest ways to trigger a ban is creating a geographic mismatch—using a proxy in Germany while your browser claims to be in California, or logging into an account from a different country than where it was created. These inconsistencies are immediately flagged by most modern platforms. Before starting any session, ensure your proxy location matches all your other identity signals. This means: - **Browser timezone**: Set to match your proxy's timezone - **Language preferences**: Configure browser language to match the proxy location - **Currency and shipping**: If you're using a UK proxy, set currency to GBP and have UK shipping addresses on file - **Device time**: Ensure your system clock matches your proxy location A concrete example: if you're targeting a US-based sneaker release, your browser should show US English, USD pricing, US shipping addresses, and your proxy should exit from a US location. Any deviation—proxy in Virginia but currency set to GBP—creates a mismatch that sophisticated systems flag. This extends to session consistency. If you create an account while using a German proxy, don't switch to a Brazilian proxy for your next session without expecting elevated scrutiny. Geographic stability matters. ## Rule 4: Rotate IPs Proactively, Not Reactively People often wait until an IP gets banned before switching—but by then, the damage is done. The ban itself is a data point that tells the platform something was wrong with that identity. A better approach is rotating IPs before you hit any trouble. The key is implementing healthy rotation schedules that feel natural rather than reactive. Change IPs after reaching a threshold of activity—not when you're already blocked. Good triggers for rotation include: - After 50-100 significant actions (logins, purchases, posts) - When you notice increased latency or captchas appearing - After any suspicious activity warnings - At regular intervals even without triggers For residential proxies, this means using a diverse pool and cycling through it regularly. For datacenter proxies, which are easier to detect, rotation becomes even more critical—switch IPs every session or even mid-session for high-risk activities. The goal is ensuring no single IP carries enough behavioral data to create a profile that platforms can flag. By rotating before you're banned, you're distributing your activity across many identities, each with less suspicious data attached. ## Rule 5: Use Session Isolation and Never Reuse Burned Credentials Once an IP or account is flagged, it's essentially burned. Using it again—even months later—carries significant risk because platforms maintain long-term records of flagged identities. The worst thing you can do is continue using credentials or IPs that have already triggered warnings. Session isolation means maintaining strict separation between different identities. Never log into multiple accounts from the same IP without explicit isolation. Don't use the same email, phone number, or authentication method across identities that should be separate. Each session should have its own dedicated IP, browser profile, and identity data. When an IP gets flagged, retire it immediately and permanently. Don't try to use it again for any purpose—the risk isn't worth the savings. Similarly, if an account gets banned, don't create a new account using the same recovery email or phone number. Platforms are increasingly good at linking these identities. For teams managing multiple accounts, this means maintaining separate browser profiles, distinct payment methods where possible, and clear documentation of which IP ranges are associated with which accounts. ## How Styxproxy Helps You Stay Safe At Styxproxy, we've built ban prevention directly into our infrastructure. Our proxy management includes automatic IP rotation based on usage patterns, residential IP pools with established histories that don't require manual warming, and geographic targeting that automatically aligns with your session data. We monitor for early warning signs and can automatically flag or rotate IPs showing any suspicious activity patterns. The reality is that proxy bans are almost always preventable with the right approach to timing, behavior, and infrastructure. By following these five rules—warming up IPs, respecting rate limits, matching session data, rotating proactively, and maintaining strict session isolation—you'll dramatically reduce your ban risk across any platform. title: Mobile 4G Proxies: The Underdog of Ad Verification
body: When ad fraud detection teams build their proxy infrastructure, they typically reach for residential IPs first. While the industry obsesses over residential bandwidth, mobile 4G proxies have been quietly delivering superior results for ad verification—at a fraction of the cost. It's time to give this underdog its due. ## What Makes Mobile 4G Proxies Different Mobile 4G proxies route traffic through real mobile devices connected to cellular networks. These aren't data centers in disguise or residential broadband connections—they're actual smartphones and tablets on LTE/4G networks from carriers like AT&T, Verizon, T-Mobile, and their subsidiaries worldwide. The key difference lies in how these IPs function at the network level. When you use a mobile 4G proxy, your requests appear to come from a device on a cellular network. That distinction matters enormously to platforms and publishers who are trying to distinguish legitimate human traffic from bots. Here's why: cellular networks operate completely differently from wired internet. IP addresses on mobile networks are assigned by carrier-grade NAT (Network Address Translation) systems. Multiple users share single IP pools. IP addresses rotate naturally as devices move between cell towers. These aren't bugs—they're features that make mobile traffic incredibly difficult to fake at scale. ## The Sticky IP Advantage: Consistency Without the Churn Now let's talk about what actually matters for ad verification work: session stability. Residential proxies have a notorious problem called "churn." Because they rely on home broadband connections, residential IPs are constantly cycling. Users disconnect, reboot routers, or simply stop using their internet for hours. Each time that happens, your verification session dies and you get a new IP—potentially from a completely different geographic area, different ISP, and different subnet. For ad verification, this is a nightmare. You're trying to establish that a particular IP address is legitimately viewing an ad, and suddenly you're on a different IP entirely. Your session integrity breaks. Your data becomes unreliable. You're left wondering whether the ad actually rendered or whether you just got switched to a different user's connection mid-session. Mobile 4G proxies solve this with their sticky IP capability. When you establish a session on a mobile proxy, that connection persists for extended periods—often hours or even days. The IP stays stable because cellular devices maintain persistent connections to carrier networks. They don't disconnect when you stop actively browsing. They don't rotate IPs based on DHCP lease expirations the way residential broadband does. This stability is invaluable for verification workflows that need to: - Complete multi-page conversion funnels without session breaks - Verify that ads render correctly over time - Monitor user journeys from impression through click-through to conversion - Build reliable behavioral profiles for fraud analysis With sticky mobile IPs, your verification session stays intact from start to finish. ## Why Residential Gets All the Attention (But Doesn't Deserve It) Residential proxies dominate the conversation for one reason: they're easier to market. "Real home IPs from real people" is an easy story to tell. It's intuitive. It sounds more legitimate, even if the reality is more complicated. The truth is that residential proxy networks have significant weaknesses for ad verification: **IP Rotation is Uncontrollable**: You can't predict when an IP will rotate, making session-based verification unreliable. **Geographic Clustering**: Residential IPs cluster in populated suburban areas, leaving coverage gaps in rural regions and emerging markets. **Higher Cost**: Because residential IPs are "premium," providers charge premium prices—even though they deliver inconsistent results for verification use cases. **Fraud Flagging**: Ironically, residential proxies are now so widely used for fraudulent activities that some platforms have started flagging entire residential IP ranges as suspicious. Mobile 4G proxies sidestep these issues. They're more affordable per IP. They provide broader geographic coverage through carrier partnerships. And because they're used primarily for legitimate mobile browsing rather than bulk residential rotation, they're less likely to be flagged as proxy traffic in the first place. ## Real-World Verification Scenarios Consider these common ad verification challenges: **Viewability Measurement**: You need to confirm that an ad was actually in-view for the required time threshold. With residential proxies, the connection might drop mid-measurement. With sticky mobile 4G, your session stays active until you've collected the full viewability data. **Geo-Targeting Validation**: You're checking whether an advertiser's geo-targeting is working correctly across different regions. Mobile proxies let you maintain consistent sessions while testing different geographic entry points—without triggering the flag that you're "rotating IPs" across locations. **Fraud Detection Calibration**: Building a fraud detection model requires understanding what legitimate mobile traffic looks like. Mobile 4G proxies give you clean, realistic cellular traffic patterns that are far more difficult for fraudsters to mimic than residential connections. **Competitive Intelligence**: Monitoring competitor ad placement over time requires sustained access. Mobile sticky sessions let you maintain monitoring positions without constant re-authentication or session rebuilding. ## The Cost Equation Here's a number that should make every ad tech team pay attention: mobile 4G proxies typically cost 40-60% less than equivalent residential proxy capacity. For teams running high-volume verification campaigns, that's a significant budget shift. But the real savings go beyond per-IP costs. When your sessions don't break, you waste less time on retries. When your data is reliable, you need less of it to make confident decisions. When your infrastructure is stable, your engineering team spends less time debugging connection issues. ## When Mobile 4G Isn't the Answer Full disclosure: mobile 4G proxies aren't universally superior. There are cases where residential still makes sense: - Applications requiring precise ISP-level targeting - Scenarios needing IP addresses from specific residential ISPs rather than carriers - Tests that specifically need to simulate home broadband user behavior But for the majority of ad verification workflows—impression measurement, viewability tracking, fraud analysis, and conversion verification—mobile 4G proxies deliver better results at lower cost. ## The Bottom Line The proxy industry has been selling you a story. title: What is an ISP Proxy?
body: An ISP proxy is a residential proxy IP address that comes from an Internet Service Provider but is allocated to a commercial data center. You get the legitimacy of a residential IP—the kind websites see as "real people"—without needing a physical device in someone's home. That's the short answer. If you want to understand why this matters, read on. ## How ISP Proxies Work When you browse the web, your connection carries an IP address. That IP tells every server you visit who you are and where you're connecting from. - **Residential IPs** come from ISPs like Comcast, AT&T, or local fiber providers. They belong to actual households. Sites trust them because they represent real people with real contracts. - **Data center IPs** come from cloud providers like AWS, DigitalOcean, or dedicated hosting companies. They're fast and cheap, but sites can easily identify them and often block them. - **ISP proxies** sit in the middle. They're data center IPs on paper, but the IP blocks are registered to consumer ISPs. To a website, it looks like a home user. In practice, it performs like a data center. You route your traffic through these IPs. Your actual IP stays hidden. The destination site sees the ISP proxy's address instead. ## Why the Distinction Matters Here's the core problem: the internet was built on trust. When servers see a connection request, they make decisions based on what that IP "should" be. Data center IPs are easy to spot. They're allocated in blocks to cloud providers. Any competent anti-fraud system can identify them in milliseconds. Once identified, they're often rate-limited or blocked outright. Residential IPs have history. They're tied to real addresses, real names, real billing accounts. An IP from a Comcast residential block in Ohio has thousands of hours of legitimate browsing behind it. It "proves" you're a real person in a real location. ISP proxies take that residential reputation and package it in a data center delivery method. The IPs aren't from someone's home router, but they're registered to the same ISP that provides home internet. That's the trick. ## What You Can Do With ISP Proxies - **Access price aggregation tools** without getting blocked by anti-scraping measures - **Verify ads** across different geographic locations - **Run account management** tasks that require appearing as a regular consumer - **Bypass basic geo-restrictions** on content that checks IP location - **Test localized features** of your own applications from different IP ranges - **Sneaker copping** and limited-release drops where retail sites check for residential IPs - **Market research** that requires seeing localized search results and landing pages ## Common Use Cases **E-commerce and retail** Check product availability and pricing across regions. Sites often show different inventory or prices based on location. ISP proxies let you see what users in those locations see. This is critical for competitive intelligence in retail. **Ad verification** Confirm your ads display correctly in specific markets. Some ad networks show different creatives based on user location. You need residential-grade IPs to verify what's actually being served. Fake residential IPs get you banned from verification platforms. **SEO monitoring** Track how your pages rank in different geographic results. Google personalization is aggressive—your US search results might differ wildly from what someone in Germany sees. ISP proxies let you see localized SERPs without triggering Google's bot detection. **Social media management** Manage multiple accounts without triggering automated bans. Platforms flag suspicious logins from data center IPs. ISP proxies look like normal home connections. This applies to Twitter, Instagram, TikTok, LinkedIn—any platform with aggressive automation detection. **Travel and ticketing** Access flight and hotel pricing as it appears to users in different countries. Prices vary by market. ISP proxies let you check fares from the perspective of a user in that region. ## ISP vs. Mobile vs. Data Center | Type | Speed | Trust Level | Cost | Best For | |------|-------|-------------|------|----------| | ISP Proxy | Fast | High | Medium | Most automation tasks | | Mobile 4G | Medium | Very High | High | Hard-to-scrape targets | | Data Center | Very Fast | Low | Low | High-volume, low-risk tasks | ISP proxies give you the best balance. You get speed close to data center, trust closer to residential. The key difference from mobile: mobile IPs come from cellular networks. They're even harder to detect because they belong to carriers with massive user bases. But mobile is slower and more expensive. For most automation tasks, ISP proxies hit the sweet spot. ## How Traffic Flows Through an ISP Proxy Here's what happens when you use an ISP proxy: 1. Your request goes to the proxy server (a machine in a data center) 2. The proxy server opens a connection to your target website 3. The target sees the ISP proxy's IP address, not yours 4. The response comes back through the same proxy 5. The proxy forwards the response to you This happens at the network level. Your application doesn't need to know anything special—it just connects to the proxy endpoint instead of directly to the target. ## Authentication Most ISP proxy providers offer username/password authentication. Here's what a typical curl request looks like: ```bash curl -x "http://username:password@isp-proxy-provider:port" \ -L "https://httpbin.org/headers" ``` Some providers offer IP authentication—whitelist your server IP and skip credentials entirely. IP auth is simpler to integrate into automated systems. Your server makes the request, the provider checks that the source IP matches your whitelist, and routes traffic accordingly. If you're building serious automation, IP auth is preferred. It means one less credential to manage, one less thing that can fail. ## What ISP Proxies Won't Do They're not magic. If a site uses aggressive fingerprinting (checking browser canvas, fonts, WebGL renderer, behavioral patterns), an IP alone won't help. You still need a solid fingerprinting solution on top. They won't make your traffic free from blocks on sites with heavy anti-bot measures. Some targets are simply difficult, regardless of your IP type. If someone has invested serious money in anti-bot infrastructure, they'll catch you eventually. They aren't as trustworthy as mobile 4G proxies for the hardest targets. If you're hitting something that aggressively bans residential, you might need mobile. The mobile carriers have massive IP pools with millions of users. There's more "noise" to hide in. ## Finding the Right Provider Things that matter: - **IP quality**: Clean IPs with no prior abuse history. Ask about their sourcing. Some providers buy cheap IP blocks that are already burned. - **Geographic coverage**: Do they have IPs in the regions you need? Not all providers have global coverage. - **Rotation options**: Static (sticky sessions) or rotating? Static is better for login sessions. Rotating is better for scraping. - **Support**: Can you reach someone when something breaks? Providers that only offer ticket support are risky for production workloads. - **Protocol support**: SOCKS5, HTTP, HTTPS—make sure your tooling works with what they offer. Avoid providers that oversell their IP pools. If 100 people are using the same IP for scraping, it's going to get burned fast. Either the IPs are burned, the network is congested, or support is nonexistent. This is a case where paying more usually saves money. **Not rotating IPs** Using the same IP for thousands of requests will get it banned. body: If you've ever tried to buy sneakers online only to watch them sell out in seconds, or scraped a website only to get blocked after a few requests, you've already bumped into the proxy world. The difference between residential and datacenter proxies can make or break your project—and most people don't find out which one they need until they've already wasted money on the wrong one. Let's break it down in plain English so you can stop guessing and start succeeding. ## What Are Residential Proxies? Residential proxies are IP addresses that belong to real devices in homes—laptops, smartphones, WiFi routers. When you use a residential proxy, websites see your traffic as coming from an actual person in a real location. That's because these IPs are assigned by internet service providers (ISPs) to homeowners. Here's why that matters: websites trust residential IPs. A lot. When Netflix, Amazon, or any major platform sees a residential IP, they're more likely to believe it's a legitimate user rather than a bot. That said, datacenter proxies have their place. For tasks that don't require stealth—like quick data collection from permissive sites, or internal testing—they can be incredibly cost-effective. At first, everything works beautifully. Then, 47 requests in, you get hit with a captcha. Then another. Then your IP is banned entirely. What happened? The website noticed patterns. Datacenter IPs don't behave like real humans—they make requests too fast, too consistently, from IP ranges that don't belong to regular consumers. Real people browse erratically. They pause, scroll, click around. Bots are efficient. And efficiency is exactly what detection systems are looking for. Residential proxies solve this naturally. Real devices have realistic browsing patterns baked in. They're also spread across the globe in ways that match actual user demographics. When a website sees a residential IP from Brooklyn, it's just another customer. When it sees an IP from a known AWS range, it's a red flag. This is why sneaker groups, ticket resellers, and social media marketers almost exclusively use residential proxies. The math is simple: spending $50 more on better proxies beats spending $500 on a setup that doesn't work. ## When to Use Residential Proxies If you're doing anything where getting caught means failure, residential is the only choice. title: Proxy Rotation: What It Is and Why It Matters
body: If you've ever tried to scrape a website at scale, cop sneakers, or run automated tools, you've hit a wall. Same IP making too many requests? Rate limits. CAPTCHA blocks. Bans. That's where proxy rotation comes in. ## What is Proxy Rotation and How Does It Work? Proxy rotation is the practice of cycling through multiple IP addresses with each request—or at regular intervals—so no single IP gets flagged for overuse. Instead of sending 1,000 requests from one IP (which triggers defenses instantly), you route those requests through a pool of 1,000 different IPs. The target website sees varied traffic from diverse sources, making it much harder to detect and block your automation. **How it works:** - Your requests go through a proxy pool - Each request gets assigned a new IP (or you rotate on a schedule) - The destination site sees different "visitors" each time - You avoid triggering rate limits and blocks This is essential for any operation that needs to act like multiple users—which is most automation tasks. ## Types of Proxy Rotation ### 1. Per-Request Rotation Every single HTTP request uses a different IP from the pool. This maximizes diversity and minimizes detection. Best for: high-volume scraping, data collection, aggressive automation. ### 2. Time-Based Rotation IPs switch at set intervals—every 30 seconds, every minute, etc. You get consistency within each window, but rotate before blocks accumulate. Best for: tasks that need session continuity but can't risk long-running sessions. ### 3. Smart/Rotating Session Rotation The system monitors IP health and rotates only when needed—after a block, slow response, or error. This balances efficiency with reliability. Best for: production-grade operations where you can't afford unnecessary rotation or failures. ### 4. Geographic Rotation You target specific countries or cities. Useful for location-specific content, localized scraping, or testing geo-restricted features. ### 5. Round-Robin Rotation Cycles through IPs in sequence: 1, 2, 3, 4... then back to 1. Simple, predictable, works when you just need distribution without any smarts. ### 6. Weighted Rotation Some IPs perform better than others. Weighted rotation sends more traffic to faster, more reliable IPs and less to slower ones. Best for: optimizing performance when you have a mixed-quality pool. ## Benefits of Using Rotating Proxies - **Avoid rate limits.** Sites limit how many requests come from one IP. Rotation spreads the load. - **Bypass blocks and CAPTCHAs.** Even if one IP gets flagged, the next request uses a clean one. - **Scale operations.** Run thousands of concurrent requests without getting banned in minutes. - **Access geo-restricted content.** Rotate through IPs in different regions to get location-specific data. - **Improved reliability.** When one IP fails, you automatically switch to the next—no manual intervention. - **Maintain anonymity.** Diverse IPs make it much harder to trace activity back to you. - **Better success rates.** With enough IPs in rotation, you maintain consistent success even when sites tighten defenses. - **Cost efficiency.** You don't need to keep buying new IPs after bans—the pool keeps rotating through clean ones. ## Rotating vs Sticky Proxies: Which to Choose? This is the most common question, and the answer depends on your use case. **Sticky (Static) Sessions** - One IP persists for the duration of a session - Good for: logging into accounts, maintaining cookies, checkout flows, anything that needs a consistent identity - Example: Completing a sneaker checkout—your session must look like one user from start to finish - Maintains cookies, session tokens, and authentication state - Looks more like a real human user to the target site **Rotating Proxies** - IP changes with each request or on a schedule - Good for: scraping, rank tracking, mass account creation, high-volume data collection - Example: Crawling 10,000 product pages—each page needs a fresh IP to avoid detection - Maximizes anonymity and avoids rate limits - Works best when you don't need session continuity **When to use which:** - Use sticky when you need session continuity (login, checkout, authenticated actions) - Use rotating when you need volume and anonymity (scraping, testing, data mining) - Use smart rotation when you want the best of both—rotate on failure, stay sticky when things work - Consider a hybrid: sticky for critical flows, rotating for everything else Many tools let you switch between modes. Advanced setups use sticky sessions for critical flows and rotate for everything else. ## Common Use Cases for Rotating Proxies ### Web Scraping at Scale When you need to collect data from thousands of pages, rotation is non-negotiable. Without it, you get blocked after a few dozen pages. ### Sneaker Copping Sneaker sites actively block bots. Rotating residential proxies give you the best chance of securing a checkout spot before the site sells out. ### Price Aggregation Travel sites, e-commerce platforms, and ticket sellers often show different prices based on location. Rotate through IPs to gather competitive pricing data. ### SEO Monitoring Track search rankings from different geographic locations. Rotate IPs to avoid getting flagged by search engines when checking many keywords. ### Ad Verification Check that your ads are displaying correctly across different regions and devices. Rotation helps you see what real users in those locations see. ### Account Creation Automating new accounts? Sites often block mass registration from single IPs. Rotation lets you scale account creation without immediate bans. ## How to Implement Proxy Rotation ### 1. Choose a Proxy Provider You need a pool. Options include: - **Datacenter proxies:** Fast, cheap, easier to detect. Fine for low-risk tasks. - **Residential proxies:** IPs from real ISPs, harder to block, more expensive. Best for serious scraping and sneaker ops. - **Mobile proxies:** Even harder to detect, rotates through mobile carrier IPs. Highest success rate but costliest. ### 2. Set Up Rotation Logic Most providers give you an endpoint that automatically rotates. You send requests to a single URL, and their system assigns different IPs. For more control: - **Backend code:** Track which IPs work, rotate after X requests or Y errors - **Proxy management tools:** Built-in rotation, health checks, geotargeting ### 3. Handle Failures Gracefully - Retry with a new IP on failure - Log which IPs are blocked or slow - Implement backoff when you hit rate limits - Keep a "cool" list of flagged IPs and avoid them for a while ### 4. Tune Your Settings - Start with per-request rotation - If you're getting blocked, increase pool size - If you need session continuity, switch to sticky mode - Monitor success rates and adjust rotation frequency The right setup is whatever keeps you running without blocks. Test, measure, iterate. ## Common Mistakes to Avoid - **Rotating too fast.** Switching IPs every request can look suspicious. Find the sweet spot. - **Ignoring IP quality.** A pool of banned IPs is useless. Monitor health and refresh your pool. - **No error handling.** When rotation fails, your whole operation stops. Build in retries and fallbacks. - **Using the wrong proxy type.** Datacenter IPs won't work against protected targets. Match proxy type to your threat level. - **Not testing locally.** Always verify your rotation works before going to production. ## Styxproxy: Smart Rotation for Every Need Styxproxy gives you both rotating and sticky sessions in one platform. Need per-request rotation for your scraper? Done. Need sticky sessions to complete a checkout? We handle that too. title: Proxy Authentication Methods Explained: IP Whitelist vs Username/Password

title: HTTP vs SOCKS5 vs HTTPS Proxies: Complete Comparison
body: If you have ever shopped for proxies and seen protocols like HTTP, HTTPS, and SOCKS5 listed side by side, you might have wondered whether they are mostly the same thing with different names. They are not. HTTP Proxy An HTTP proxy understands the HTTP protocol. It can read and modify request headers, cache responses, and apply rules like access control. It only works with HTTP traffic (HTTPS requires a CONNECT-method HTTP proxy). HTTPS Proxy An HTTPS proxy uses the CONNECT method to establish a TCP tunnel through the proxy. End-to-end TLS is preserved — the proxy never sees your plaintext. Best for privacy-sensitive workloads. SOCKS5 Proxy SOCKS5 is protocol-agnostic. It works at the TCP/UDP level and does not care whether traffic is HTTP, SMTP, BitTorrent, or anything else. It is the most flexible choice — and the slowest per-request because there is no protocol optimization. Which One Should You Use? Browser/web scraping → HTTP or HTTPS (whichever your tool supports) General TCP apps (email clients, games, custom tools) → SOCKS5 Privacy-first → HTTPS or SOCKS5 over TLS Styxproxy supports all three out of the box — pick whichever your tool needs.

title: Residential vs Datacenter Proxies: Which Should You Choose?
body: When it comes to choosing proxy services, the debate between residential and datacenter proxies is one of the most most important decisions you will make. Both have distinct advantages, and understanding them is critical for getting the most out of your proxy investment. What Are Residential Proxies? Residential proxies are IP addresses assigned by Internet Service Providers (ISPs) to real devices in actual households. When you use a residential proxy, websites see your requests as coming from a genuine home user, making them significantly harder to detect and block. What Are Datacenter Proxies? Datacenter proxies, on the other hand, are generated from cloud servers and data centers. They offer blazing-fast speeds and are significantly cheaper, but websites can more easily identify them as non-residential traffic. Key Differences Detection Rate: Residential proxies have a much lower detection rate. Speed: Datacenter proxies are typically 5-10x faster. Cost: Datacenter proxies are 60-80% cheaper. Geotargeting: Residential proxies offer more precise geographic targeting. Which Should You Choose? For Nigerian web scraping and market research, residential proxies are highly recommended due to their ability to access local content without triggering anti-bot measures. For high-volume, speed-critical tasks like SEO monitoring or price aggregation, datacenter proxies offer the best value.
